items.prompt: What does a bounded context guarantee?
choices: That every module in it runs on the same server
That a term means one consistent thing inside it, and one group owns its data
That the code inside it has no bugs
That it can never talk to any other part of the system
items.explanation: A bounded context is defined by consistent meaning and clear ownership inside its boundary, not by deployment topology or by isolation from every other part of the system — contexts still talk to each other, just through a boundary instead of a shared internal state.
items.reference:
Bounded context = one consistent meaning for a term + one owner for the data behind it, inside a line you draw.

Why: this is what makes a service boundary meaningful instead of just a folder that got its own deploy pipeline.

items.prompt: The word "Order" means something slightly different in the Orders module than it does in the Reporting module. Is that a problem to fix before splitting the monolith?
choices: Yes — every module must use identical definitions for every term
No — different bounded contexts are allowed to define the same word differently, as long as each is internally consistent
Yes, but only if the two modules share a database table
No, because naming doesn't matter for coupling
items.explanation: Different bounded contexts legitimately model the same real-world word differently for their own purposes (a purchase with line items vs. a flattened analytics row) — that's normal and expected, not a defect to unify away.
items.reference:
Bounded context = one consistent meaning for a term + one owner for the data behind it, inside a line you draw.

Why: this is what makes a service boundary meaningful instead of just a folder that got its own deploy pipeline.

items.prompt: A monolith has never had its modules formally named as "bounded contexts." Does that mean bounded contexts don't exist in it yet?
choices: Correct — bounded contexts only exist once you name and diagram them
No — the boundaries already exist implicitly in how the code and data are organized; splitting just makes them explicit and enforced
Correct — a monolith by definition has exactly one bounded context
No, because bounded contexts only apply to microservices, not monoliths
items.explanation: A monolith almost always has implicit bounded contexts already, just unenforced — the act of extracting services makes an existing seam explicit (with a real API and separate deploys) rather than inventing a boundary from nothing.
items.reference:
Bounded context = one consistent meaning for a term + one owner for the data behind it, inside a line you draw.

Why: this is what makes a service boundary meaningful instead of just a folder that got its own deploy pipeline.

items.prompt: What's the ideal combination of coupling and cohesion for a candidate service boundary?
choices: High coupling out, high cohesion in
Low coupling out, low cohesion in
Low coupling out, high cohesion in
High coupling out, low cohesion in
items.explanation: A good boundary depends little on modules outside it (low coupling out) while the modules inside it depend heavily on each other (high cohesion in) — that combination is what holds together as one self-contained service.
items.reference:
Couplingdepends on outside modules
Cohesiondepends on modules inside the group

Why: low coupling out + high cohesion in is the shape that survives being cut into its own service.

items.prompt: Two modules share a database table, reading and writing it directly. What does that indicate?
choices: Strong cohesion between the two modules
Strong coupling — the strongest signal there is, since no API boundary was ever enforced
Nothing significant, since database access is always fast
That the two modules should never be split under any circumstances
items.explanation: A shared table read/written by two modules directly is the strongest coupling signal available — it means the only contract between them is an informal convention, not an enforced API, which is exactly what turns into a distributed transaction problem once split.
items.reference:
Couplingdepends on outside modules
Cohesiondepends on modules inside the group

Why: low coupling out + high cohesion in is the shape that survives being cut into its own service.

items.prompt: A candidate group of modules calls each other constantly internally, and barely calls anything outside the group. What does that describe?
choices: Low cohesion, which is bad for extraction
High cohesion and low external coupling — a good candidate boundary
High coupling, which always blocks extraction
A sign the group needs to be split further before extraction
items.explanation: Modules that lean on each other internally but rarely reach outside the group are exhibiting exactly the pattern that predicts a clean, self-contained service boundary.
items.reference:
Couplingdepends on outside modules
Cohesiondepends on modules inside the group

Why: low coupling out + high cohesion in is the shape that survives being cut into its own service.

items.prompt: A team picks its first extraction target purely by "which module do we complain about most." What's the risk in that alone?
choices: There's no risk — team pain is always correlated with clean data boundaries
The most-complained-about module might share tables or have heavy call traffic with modules staying behind, turning the split into a distributed-transaction problem
It's risky only if the module has fewer than 100 lines of code
It's risky only because complaints are subjective, not because of any technical coupling issue
items.explanation: Team pain is a real signal worth listening to, but it says nothing about whether the module's data and calls are actually self-contained — picking by pain alone, without checking coupling, is how a team ends up extracting a module that still shares a table with something left behind.
items.reference:
"Most annoying" and "cleanest boundary" are two different questions with two different answers.

Why: team pain picks a target; coupling analysis checks whether that target is safe to actually cut.

items.prompt: Co-change (files that get edited together in the same commits across module folders) is useful for finding boundaries because:
choices: It reveals hidden coupling the compiler and the schema can't show — a signal git history has that static analysis doesn't
It measures how many developers work on the module
It's the only signal that matters; shared tables and call frequency can be ignored if co-change is low
It only applies to monorepos, not monoliths
items.explanation: Co-change surfaces coupling that isn't visible in the schema or the call graph — two modules whose files always change together in the same commits are coupled in practice, even if nothing formally links them.
items.reference:
"Most annoying" and "cleanest boundary" are two different questions with two different answers.

Why: team pain picks a target; coupling analysis checks whether that target is safe to actually cut.

items.prompt: How does domain-boundary analysis relate to the strangler fig migration pattern?
choices: They're competing alternatives — you pick one or the other
Domain-boundary analysis decides WHERE to cut; strangler fig is the mechanism for HOW to cut over gradually once a boundary is chosen
Domain-boundary analysis replaces the need for a strangler fig migration entirely
Strangler fig is only for frontend routes, so it's unrelated to backend module boundaries
items.explanation: The two are complementary, not competing: coupling/cohesion analysis picks a defensible boundary to extract, and the strangler fig pattern (a routing facade, migrated incrementally) is how that chosen boundary actually gets cut over without a big-bang rewrite.
items.reference:
Where to cut (domain boundaries) and how to cut over gradually (strangler fig) are two different questions.

Why: a strangler fig migration on the wrong boundary still ends up dragging a shared-table dependency along, route by route.

items.prompt: A team runs a textbook strangler fig migration (routing facade, one route per week, full rollback per route) on a module that still shares a database table with a module staying behind. What happens?
choices: Nothing — the strangler fig pattern automatically resolves shared-table coupling
Each migrated route still needs to coordinate writes across the shared table, so the migration mechanics are clean but the underlying coupling problem persists route by route
The migration becomes impossible to start at all
The shared table automatically gets duplicated into both services
items.explanation: Strangler fig is purely a cutover mechanism — it says nothing about whether the thing being cut over is a clean boundary. A shared table dragged into the migration stays a shared table, needing a distributed transaction or a sync job on every migrated route, regardless of how gradual the rollout is.
items.reference:
Where to cut (domain boundaries) and how to cut over gradually (strangler fig) are two different questions.

Why: a strangler fig migration on the wrong boundary still ends up dragging a shared-table dependency along, route by route.

items.prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the concrete signals for finding a boundary described at this level?
choices: Shared database tables between modules
Call frequency across a proposed boundary
How many lines of code the module has
Vocabulary — whether a term means the same thing everywhere it's used
items.explanation: Lines of code says nothing about coupling or cohesion. The real signals are shared tables, cross-module call frequency, co-change in version control, and whether vocabulary stays consistent — all of them measure relationships, not size.
items.reference:
Signals: shared tables, call frequency, co-change, vocabulary. Not: file size, line count, module age.

Why: these are all measurable from the code and data as they exist today, without a design meeting.

items.prompt: Why is a shared database table considered a stronger coupling signal than call frequency?
choices: Because a call can be replaced by a well-defined API, while two modules silently sharing a table has no such natural interface to swap in
Because database calls are always slower than function calls
It isn't stronger — call frequency is always the more important signal
Because shared tables are illegal in most database engines
items.explanation: A high-frequency call across modules can be wrapped behind an API without changing behavior. A shared table has no such natural seam — both modules are directly coupled to the same schema, which is a harder and more structural form of coupling to remove.
items.reference:
Signals: shared tables, call frequency, co-change, vocabulary. Not: file size, line count, module age.

Why: these are all measurable from the code and data as they exist today, without a design meeting.

items.prompt: Two files in different module folders keep getting edited in the same commits, over and over, even though nothing in the schema or the call graph formally links them. What does that pattern suggest?
choices: Nothing — co-change is a coincidence and never worth investigating
Hidden coupling that neither the schema nor the call graph reveals, worth checking as a boundary signal
That the two files must be merged into a single file immediately
That the repository's commit history is corrupted
items.explanation: Repeated co-change across module folders is real evidence of coupling the static structure hides — two pieces of code that always change together are dependent on each other in practice, whether or not any import or table connects them on paper.
items.reference:
Signals: shared tables, call frequency, co-change, vocabulary. Not: file size, line count, module age.

Why: these are all measurable from the code and data as they exist today, without a design meeting.

items.prompt: In the weighted call graph model, why is a shared-table relationship modeled as a distinct kind of edge from a regular call edge?
choices: Because shared-table edges are always drawn in a different color for aesthetic reasons only
Because it's a structurally stronger and different kind of coupling — a call can be replaced by an API, but a shared table can't be, without one module moving first
Because the graph library requires two edge types by default
There's no real difference; it's just a labeling convention with no consequence
items.explanation: The distinction isn't cosmetic: a call edge is something an API boundary can absorb, while a shared-table edge means two modules are directly coupled to the same schema with no interface between them at all — a fundamentally harder problem to resolve.
items.reference:
Graph nodes = modules. Call edges = weighted by frequency. Shared-table edges = a separate, stronger signal.

Why: the model has to distinguish coupling kinds, or scoring collapses them into one number that hides the real risk.

items.prompt: What does a directed, weighted edge from module A to module B in this call graph represent?
choices: That module A is owned by the same team as module B
That A calls B, weighted by how often that call happens
That A and B were deployed on the same date
That A is a newer version of B
items.explanation: An edge captures a real runtime dependency — A calling into B — weighted by frequency, which is what lets the scoring step distinguish a rarely-used dependency from one that's load-bearing on every request.
items.reference:
Graph nodes = modules. Call edges = weighted by frequency. Shared-table edges = a separate, stronger signal.

Why: the model has to distinguish coupling kinds, or scoring collapses them into one number that hides the real risk.

items.prompt: What does "internal call ratio" measure for a candidate group of modules?
choices: The percentage of the company's engineers who work on that group
Of all call volume touching the group, what fraction stays inside the group versus crossing out to other modules
How many internal functions each module has, regardless of calls
The ratio of reads to writes inside the group
items.explanation: Internal call ratio is internal-call-volume divided by total call volume touching the group — high means the group mostly talks to itself; low means extracting it drags the rest of the system along on every request.
items.reference:
internal call ratio = internal / (internal + external). Read together with external shared tables, not alone.

Why: a group can game one number by growing bigger — the two numbers together prevent that.

items.prompt: A team keeps bundling more and more modules into a single "candidate boundary" specifically to push internal call ratio toward 100%. What's wrong with that strategy?
choices: Nothing is wrong — internal call ratio is the only number that matters

A large enough bundle always scores near 100% internal ratio because "internal" now includes almost everything, which just recreates the monolith under a new name without solving the original coupling problem
It's wrong only because bundles can't exceed 3 modules by convention
It's wrong because internal call ratio can never exceed 50% for real systems
items.explanation: Growing the group makes internal ratio rise almost mechanically, since more of the graph's calls now happen to fall "inside." That's gaming the metric — a bundle covering most of the monolith isn't a service boundary, it's the monolith with new packaging. The right target is the smallest group that also gets external shared tables to zero.
items.reference:
internal call ratio = internal / (internal + external). Read together with external shared tables, not alone.

Why: a group can game one number by growing bigger — the two numbers together prevent that.

items.prompt: What should the "external shared tables" count be for a genuinely clean candidate boundary?
choices: As high as possible
Zero — any table shared between a module inside the group and one outside it is a coupling the split hasn't actually resolved
Exactly one, as a sanity check
It doesn't matter as long as internal call ratio is above 50%
items.explanation: External shared tables should be zero for a clean boundary — any table still shared with something outside the group means the split hasn't removed that coupling, it's just moved it across a network line where it becomes a distributed transaction.
items.reference:
External shared tables should be zero. Any non-zero count is unresolved coupling waiting to become a distributed transaction.

Why: this is the number that catches what internal call ratio alone can miss.

items.prompt: A candidate group has a strong internal call ratio (90%) but a non-zero external shared table count. What should that tell the team?
choices: The boundary is safe to extract as-is, since 90% internal is a strong number
The boundary isn't actually clean yet — either grow the group to absorb the shared-table module, or resolve the sharing before extracting
The external shared tables number can be ignored once internal call ratio passes 80%
The two metrics always move together, so this situation can't actually happen
items.explanation: A high internal call ratio doesn't cancel out a shared table — the two metrics measure different things (call traffic vs. data ownership), and a shared table is the harder-to-remove coupling. The fix is to either widen the group to include the table's other owner or resolve the sharing (separate tables, sync via events) before cutting.
items.reference:
External shared tables should be zero. Any non-zero count is unresolved coupling waiting to become a distributed transaction.

Why: this is the number that catches what internal call ratio alone can miss.

items.prompt: In the boundary-finding method, what's the correct next step when a candidate group scores non-zero on external shared tables?
choices: Extract it anyway and fix the shared table after the split ships
Either grow the group to absorb the shared-table module, or resolve the data sharing (separate tables, sync via events) before extracting
Abandon extraction entirely and never revisit that module
Ignore the shared table if the internal call ratio is above 70%
items.explanation: A non-zero external shared table count means the boundary as drawn isn't ready. The method's next step is to either widen the boundary to include the other table owner, or resolve the sharing first — not to extract anyway and hope, and not to give up on the module permanently.
items.reference:
Method: build graph → propose group → score → if shared tables > 0, widen or resolve → extract.

Why: the method is where-to-cut; strangler fig (a separate unit) is how-to-cut-over.

items.prompt: Once a candidate group scores well (zero external shared tables, high internal call ratio), what does that group become?
choices: A permanent monolith module that should never change again
The first strangler-fig target — the mechanics of the gradual cutover itself are a separate concern from choosing where to cut
Proof that no further modules need ever be extracted
A candidate for deletion rather than extraction
items.explanation: A clean-scoring group becomes the boundary to extract first — the where. How that extraction actually happens gradually, with a routing facade and route-by-route rollback, is the strangler fig pattern's job, covered separately.
items.reference:
Method: build graph → propose group → score → if shared tables > 0, widen or resolve → extract.

Why: the method is where-to-cut; strangler fig (a separate unit) is how-to-cut-over.

items.prompt: One edge has very high call frequency but no shared table. Another has low call frequency but a shared table. Which is the bigger red flag for a candidate boundary?
choices: The high-frequency, no-shared-table edge — frequency always dominates
The low-frequency, shared-table edge — a shared table resists being split even at low traffic, while high-frequency calls with no shared data can usually be absorbed behind an API
Neither matters; only the number of modules involved matters
They're equally risky in all cases
items.explanation: Call frequency alone measures traffic, which an API can absorb regardless of volume. A shared table is a structural coupling that doesn't go away just because the traffic across it is low — it's the harder problem, and the one that turns into a distributed transaction the moment a network boundary is drawn through it.
items.reference:
High traffic on a clean interface: fine. Low traffic through a shared table: the red flag.

Why: the two signals need to be read together, not by frequency alone.

items.prompt: Catalog calls Orders 20,000 times a day for read-only price lookups, with no shared table. Should that alone disqualify Catalog+Orders as a bad idea to leave separate?
choices: Yes — any call frequency that high automatically means the two modules must be merged
No — high-frequency, read-only calls with no shared table are exactly the kind of dependency an API (or a cache) absorbs cleanly; the shared-table signal matters more
Yes, because 20,000 is an arbitrary threshold above which merging is always required
No, because call frequency is never a meaningful signal at all
items.explanation: High call frequency by itself isn't disqualifying — what matters is whether the call is the kind of dependency an interface can absorb. A read-only lookup with no shared table is exactly that kind; a low-frequency call through a shared table is not.
items.reference:
High traffic on a clean interface: fine. Low traffic through a shared table: the red flag.

Why: the two signals need to be read together, not by frequency alone.

items.prompt: Why is "vocabulary drift" (a term meaning subtly different things in different parts of the same module) treated as a boundary signal, not just a naming-convention issue?
choices: Because inconsistent naming is always a bug that must be fixed before anything else
Because a term quietly meaning two different things in one place is often marking a seam nobody has drawn yet — a sign two bounded contexts are tangled inside what looks like one module
Because vocabulary has no relationship to coupling or cohesion at all
Because it means the module's tests are incomplete
items.explanation: When a single module quietly uses one word to mean two different things depending on which code path you're in, that's often evidence two distinct bounded contexts are living inside what's nominally one module — the inconsistency is a symptom of an undrawn boundary, not a cosmetic naming slip.
items.reference:
Co-change (git history) and vocabulary drift are signals a call graph alone can't show.

Why: both point at coupling or a hidden boundary that structural analysis alone misses.

items.prompt: Co-change analysis (which files change together in commits) is best understood as:
choices: A replacement for the call graph and shared-table analysis — you only need one of the three
An additional signal that surfaces coupling the schema and the call graph don't capture, meant to be read alongside them, not instead of them
Irrelevant once a codebase has good test coverage
Only useful for repositories with fewer than 10 contributors
items.explanation: Co-change is complementary, not a substitute — it catches coupling that neither the schema (shared tables) nor the runtime call graph shows, such as two modules whose business logic quietly depends on the same undocumented assumption and so get edited together every time that assumption changes.
items.reference:
Co-change (git history) and vocabulary drift are signals a call graph alone can't show.

Why: both point at coupling or a hidden boundary that structural analysis alone misses.

items.prompt: A candidate boundary scores perfectly on internal call ratio and external shared tables, but its files show heavy co-change with a module outside the group. What should that co-change signal make the team do?
choices: Ignore it — the two structural metrics already settled the question
Investigate before committing to the split — co-change can reveal coupling (shared assumptions, implicit contracts) the structural metrics don't capture
Automatically reject the boundary regardless of what the investigation finds
Merge the two modules permanently without further analysis
items.explanation: Structural metrics (call ratio, shared tables) don't see every kind of coupling — heavy co-change with an outside module is a real, independent signal worth investigating before trusting a boundary that otherwise looks clean, not something to override the other two metrics blindly or to dismiss outright.
items.reference:
Co-change (git history) and vocabulary drift are signals a call graph alone can't show.

Why: both point at coupling or a hidden boundary that structural analysis alone misses.

items.prompt: Implement `internalCallRatio(graph, group)`. `graph.edges` is an array of `{ from, to, callsPerDay }`. `group` is an array of module names. Return the fraction (0-1) of call volume touching the group that stays inside it (both endpoints in `group`). If no edges touch the group at all, return 1.

tests.description: fully internal group returns 1
tests.expr: expect(internalCallRatio({ edges: [{ from: 'A', to: 'B', callsPerDay: 10 }] }, ['A', 'B'])).toBe(1)

tests.description: fully external edge returns 0
tests.expr: expect(internalCallRatio({ edges: [{ from: 'A', to: 'C', callsPerDay: 10 }] }, ['A', 'B'])).toBe(0)

tests.description: mixed edges compute the correct ratio
tests.expr: expect(internalCallRatio({ edges: [{ from: 'A', to: 'B', callsPerDay: 8 }, { from: 'A', to: 'C', callsPerDay: 2 }] }, ['A', 'B'])).toBe(0.8)

tests.description: no touching edges returns 1
tests.expr: expect(internalCallRatio({ edges: [{ from: 'X', to: 'Y', callsPerDay: 5 }] }, ['A', 'B'])).toBe(1)

items.explanation: Filter to edges that touch the group at all, then sum call weight, separating the subset where both endpoints are inside the group. Dividing internal by total gives the fraction of the group's total call traffic that never leaves it — the higher this is, the more self-contained the group is as an extraction candidate.
items.reference:
internal call ratio = internal call volume / total call volume touching the group.

Why: a group with a low ratio drags the rest of the graph along on every request once extracted.

items.prompt: Implement `internalCallRatio(graph, group)` again, but this time treat it as a review sanity check: given `graph.edges` as `{ from, to, callsPerDay }` and a `group` array, it must correctly handle a group with THREE members where some edges are internal-to-internal, some are internal-to-external, and none touch the group at all (those should be ignored).

tests.description: three-member group sums internal edges correctly
tests.expr: expect(internalCallRatio({ edges: [{ from: 'A', to: 'B', callsPerDay: 5 }, { from: 'B', to: 'C', callsPerDay: 5 }, { from: 'A', to: 'D', callsPerDay: 10 }] }, ['A', 'B', 'C'])).toBe(0.5)

tests.description: edges not touching the group are ignored entirely
tests.expr: expect(internalCallRatio({ edges: [{ from: 'X', to: 'Y', callsPerDay: 99 }, { from: 'A', to: 'B', callsPerDay: 5 }] }, ['A', 'B', 'C'])).toBe(1)

tests.description: no edges at all returns 1
tests.expr: expect(internalCallRatio({ edges: [] }, ['A', 'B'])).toBe(1)

items.explanation: The logic doesn't change with group size — a Set membership check works identically for 2 or 20 modules. Edges where neither endpoint is in the group are filtered out up front so they don't distort the ratio; only edges that touch the group at all contribute to the denominator.
items.reference:
internal call ratio = internal call volume / total call volume touching the group.

Why: a group with a low ratio drags the rest of the graph along on every request once extracted.

items.prompt: Implement `externalSharedTables(graph, group)`. `graph.edges` is `{ from, to, sharedTables }` (an array of table names, possibly empty). Return a deduplicated array of every table name that appears on an edge crossing the boundary — exactly one of `from`/`to` inside `group`.

tests.description: crossing edge contributes its shared tables
tests.expr: expect(externalSharedTables({ edges: [{ from: 'A', to: 'C', sharedTables: ['t1'] }] }, ['A', 'B'])).toEqual(['t1'])

tests.description: fully internal edge contributes nothing, even with sharedTables set
tests.expr: expect(externalSharedTables({ edges: [{ from: 'A', to: 'B', sharedTables: ['t1'] }] }, ['A', 'B'])).toEqual([])

tests.description: fully external edge contributes nothing
tests.expr: expect(externalSharedTables({ edges: [{ from: 'C', to: 'D', sharedTables: ['t1'] }] }, ['A', 'B'])).toEqual([])

tests.description: duplicate table names across multiple crossing edges are deduplicated
tests.expr: expect(externalSharedTables({ edges: [{ from: 'A', to: 'C', sharedTables: ['t1'] }, { from: 'B', to: 'D', sharedTables: ['t1'] }] }, ['A', 'B']).length).toBe(1)

items.explanation: `fromIn !== toIn` is true exactly when one endpoint is inside the group and one is outside — a crossing edge. Only crossing edges' shared tables are collected, using a Set to dedupe across multiple crossing edges that mention the same table.
items.reference:
external shared tables = tables touched by edges where exactly one endpoint is inside the group.

Why: non-zero means the split hasn't actually removed the coupling, just relocated it.

items.prompt: Implement `externalSharedTables(graph, group)` a third way, and confirm it handles an edge whose `sharedTables` array has MULTIPLE table names, all of which must be reported if that edge crosses the boundary.

tests.description: a crossing edge with two shared tables reports both
tests.expr: expect(externalSharedTables({ edges: [{ from: 'A', to: 'C', sharedTables: ['t1', 't2'] }] }, ['A', 'B']).sort()).toEqual(['t1', 't2'])

tests.description: an internal edge with two shared tables reports neither
tests.expr: expect(externalSharedTables({ edges: [{ from: 'A', to: 'B', sharedTables: ['t1', 't2'] }] }, ['A', 'B'])).toEqual([])

items.explanation: The inner `for...of` loop over `edge.sharedTables` means every table name on a crossing edge gets added to the result set, not just the first one — a real edge can legitimately share more than one table with the module on the other side of the boundary.
items.reference:
external shared tables = tables touched by edges where exactly one endpoint is inside the group.

Why: non-zero means the split hasn't actually removed the coupling, just relocated it.

items.prompt: Implement `externalSharedTables(graph, group)` once more, but this time make sure it correctly returns an empty array (not undefined, not null) when the group has zero external coupling, since a review script will call `.length` on the result unconditionally.

tests.description: clean group returns an empty array, not null/undefined
tests.expr: expect(externalSharedTables({ edges: [{ from: 'A', to: 'B', sharedTables: [] }] }, ['A', 'B'])).toEqual([])

tests.description: empty graph returns an empty array
tests.expr: expect(externalSharedTables({ edges: [] }, ['A', 'B'])).toEqual([])

tests.description: result length can be called safely on a clean group
tests.expr: expect(externalSharedTables({ edges: [{ from: 'A', to: 'B', sharedTables: [] }] }, ['A', 'B']).length).toBe(0)

items.explanation: Spreading a `Set` (even an empty one) into an array with `[...shared]` always produces a real array — never null or undefined — so a caller can safely check `.length === 0` as the "clean boundary" condition without a null check first.
items.reference:
external shared tables = tables touched by edges where exactly one endpoint is inside the group.

Why: non-zero means the split hasn't actually removed the coupling, just relocated it.

items.prompt: Given working `internalCallRatio(graph, group)` and `externalSharedTables(graph, group)` functions (assume they exist and work correctly), implement `scoreBoundary(graph, group)` that returns `{ internalCallRatio, externalSharedTables, verdict }`, where `internalCallRatio` is rounded to 2 decimal places and `verdict` is `"clean"` when there are zero external shared tables, or `"blocked"` otherwise.

tests.description: clean group gets verdict 'clean'
tests.expr: expect(scoreBoundary({ edges: [{ from: 'A', to: 'B', callsPerDay: 10, sharedTables: [] }] }, ['A', 'B']).verdict).toBe('clean')

tests.description: group with a crossing shared table gets verdict 'blocked'
tests.expr: expect(scoreBoundary({ edges: [{ from: 'A', to: 'C', callsPerDay: 10, sharedTables: ['t1'] }] }, ['A', 'B']).verdict).toBe('blocked')

tests.description: internalCallRatio is rounded to 2 decimal places
tests.expr: expect(scoreBoundary({ edges: [{ from: 'A', to: 'B', callsPerDay: 1, sharedTables: [] }, { from: 'A', to: 'C', callsPerDay: 2, sharedTables: [] }] }, ['A', 'B']).internalCallRatio).toBe(0.33)

items.explanation: `scoreBoundary` composes the two lower-level metrics into one review-ready object: round the ratio for readability, keep the raw table list for evidence, and derive a one-word verdict directly from whether any shared tables crossed the line — the single fact that decides if the boundary is ready.
items.reference:
scoreBoundary composes internalCallRatio + externalSharedTables into one review-ready verdict.

Why: a review needs one number and one sentence, not two separate function calls to reconstruct by hand.

items.prompt: Implement `compareBoundaries(graph, groups)` which takes an array of candidate groups (each an array of module names) and, using the given `scoreBoundary` function, returns the group (not the score object, the group itself) with the best score — defined as: 'clean' verdict beats 'blocked' verdict regardless of ratio, and among groups with the same verdict, higher internalCallRatio wins.

tests.description: clean group beats blocked group even with lower ratio
tests.expr: expect(compareBoundaries({ edges: [{ from: 'A', to: 'B', callsPerDay: 1, sharedTables: [] }, { from: 'C', to: 'D', callsPerDay: 100, sharedTables: ['t1'] }, { from: 'C', to: 'E', callsPerDay: 100, sharedTables: [] }] }, [['A', 'B'], ['C', 'D']])).toEqual(['A', 'B'])

tests.description: among two clean groups, higher internal ratio wins
tests.expr: expect(compareBoundaries({ edges: [{ from: 'A', to: 'B', callsPerDay: 10, sharedTables: [] }, { from: 'C', to: 'D', callsPerDay: 5, sharedTables: [] }, { from: 'C', to: 'X', callsPerDay: 5, sharedTables: [] }] }, [['A', 'B'], ['C', 'D']])).toEqual(['A', 'B'])

items.explanation: The comparison logic mirrors how a review should reason: verdict is the gate (a blocked boundary loses to any clean one no matter its ratio), and ratio is only the tiebreaker among boundaries that already cleared the gate — exactly the priority L2 argued for (shared tables over raw call ratio).

Why: a review needs one number and one sentence, not two separate function calls to reconstruct by hand.

items.prompt: Using the given `scoreBoundary` function, implement `firstCleanBoundary(graph, groups)` that returns the FIRST group in the `groups` array (in original order) whose verdict is `'clean'`, or `null` if none qualify — this models a review checking candidates in the team's preferred priority order rather than picking the globally best one.

tests.description: returns the first clean group, skipping earlier blocked ones
tests.expr: expect(firstCleanBoundary({ edges: [{ from: 'A', to: 'X', callsPerDay: 5, sharedTables: ['t1'] }, { from: 'C', to: 'D', callsPerDay: 5, sharedTables: [] }] }, [['A', 'B'], ['C', 'D']])).toEqual(['C', 'D'])

tests.description: returns null when no group is clean
tests.expr: expect(firstCleanBoundary({ edges: [{ from: 'A', to: 'X', callsPerDay: 5, sharedTables: ['t1'] }] }, [['A', 'B']])).toBe(null)

items.explanation: This is a deliberately different reduction than `compareBoundaries` — instead of scanning every candidate to find the globally best one, it stops at the first candidate that clears the 'clean' bar, in whatever priority order the team already fed in. Both are legitimate review strategies; which one to use depends on whether order already encodes a preference (e.g. team-pain ranking) or not.

items.prompt: Implement `suggestBoundary(usage, moduleOwnership)`. `usage.tableAccess` maps table name to access count; `usage.callsFrom` maps calling module name to call count. `moduleOwnership` maps table name to its owning module. Score each module by summing (table access count, for tables it owns) plus (caller count * 0.5, for modules that call it). Return `{ module, confidence }` where `module` is the highest-scoring module and `confidence` is its score divided by the total of all scores, rounded to 2 decimals. Return `{ module: null, confidence: 0 }` if there's no data.

tests.description: table access dominates when there are no callers
tests.expr: expect(suggestBoundary({ tableAccess: { orders_t: 10 }, callsFrom: {} }, { orders_t: 'Orders' }).module).toBe('Orders')

tests.description: combines table ownership and caller weight correctly
tests.expr: expect(suggestBoundary({ tableAccess: { shipping_t: 40, orders_t: 5 }, callsFrom: { Shipping: 30, Orders: 2 } }, { shipping_t: 'Shipping', orders_t: 'Orders' }).module).toBe('Shipping')

tests.description: no data returns null module and 0 confidence
tests.expr: expect(suggestBoundary({ tableAccess: {}, callsFrom: {} }, {})).toEqual({ module: null, confidence: 0 })

items.explanation: Table ownership contributes at full weight since it reflects structural data dependency; caller counts contribute at half weight since traffic patterns are less stable evidence of true ownership. Summing both per module and picking the top score gives a defensible "this class mostly belongs here" answer with a confidence number attached.
items.reference:
suggestBoundary weighs table ownership at full value, caller counts at half value.

Why: data ownership is the more stable, structural signal; caller counts drift with current traffic.

items.prompt: Implement `suggestBoundary(usage, moduleOwnership)` again, but this time make sure a table access to a table with NO entry in `moduleOwnership` (an unmapped/unknown table) is silently ignored rather than crashing or contributing to any module's score.

tests.description: unmapped table is ignored, known table still wins
tests.expr: expect(suggestBoundary({ tableAccess: { mystery_t: 999, orders_t: 5 }, callsFrom: {} }, { orders_t: 'Orders' }).module).toBe('Orders')

tests.description: does not throw when a table has no owner mapping
tests.expr: expect(() => suggestBoundary({ tableAccess: { unmapped: 10 }, callsFrom: {} }, {})).not.toThrow()

tests.description: all-unmapped input returns null module
tests.expr: expect(suggestBoundary({ tableAccess: { unmapped: 10 }, callsFrom: {} }, {}).module).toBe(null)

items.explanation: The `if (owner)` guard before calling `bump` is what makes an unmapped table inert instead of a crash — `moduleOwnership[table]` returns `undefined` for a table with no entry, and the guard skips scoring entirely rather than trying to bump a module named `undefined`.
items.reference:
suggestBoundary weighs table ownership at full value, caller counts at half value.

Why: data ownership is the more stable, structural signal; caller counts drift with current traffic.

items.prompt: Implement `suggestBoundary(usage, moduleOwnership)` once more, applied to a genuinely ambiguous case: verify it returns a confidence STRICTLY below 0.6 (not a landslide) when table access and caller counts are split nearly evenly between two modules.

tests.description: near-even split produces low confidence, not a landslide
tests.expr: expect(suggestBoundary({ tableAccess: { a_t: 20, b_t: 18 }, callsFrom: {} }, { a_t: 'ModuleA', b_t: 'ModuleB' }).confidence < 0.6).toBeTruthy()

tests.description: near-even split still picks the higher-scoring module
tests.expr: expect(suggestBoundary({ tableAccess: { a_t: 20, b_t: 18 }, callsFrom: {} }, { a_t: 'ModuleA', b_t: 'ModuleB' }).module).toBe('ModuleA')

items.explanation: Confidence is topScore divided by the sum of all scores — when two modules are nearly tied, neither score dominates the total, so confidence lands close to 0.5 rather than near 1.0. That low confidence is itself useful review information: it flags the class as a genuinely contested case worth a human decision, not an obvious call.

Why: data ownership is the more stable, structural signal; caller counts drift with current traffic.

items.prompt: Implement `cohesionDensity(graph, group)`, a metric distinct from `internalCallRatio`: it ignores call volume and instead measures structural density — how many of the possible directed pairs within `group` actually have an edge between them. `group` has `n` modules, so there are `n * (n - 1)` possible directed pairs (A->B and B->A count separately). Count DISTINCT `from`-`to` pairs in `graph.edges` where both endpoints are in `group`, and return that count divided by `n * (n - 1)`. Return 0 if `group` has fewer than 2 modules.

tests.description: two modules with one directed edge out of two possible pairs gives 0.5
tests.expr: expect(cohesionDensity({ edges: [{ from: 'A', to: 'B', callsPerDay: 999 }] }, ['A', 'B'])).toBe(0.5)

tests.description: two modules with both directions present gives 1
tests.expr: expect(cohesionDensity({ edges: [{ from: 'A', to: 'B', callsPerDay: 1 }, { from: 'B', to: 'A', callsPerDay: 1 }] }, ['A', 'B'])).toBe(1)

tests.description: a group of fewer than 2 modules returns 0
tests.expr: expect(cohesionDensity({ edges: [] }, ['A'])).toBe(0)

tests.description: duplicate edges for the same pair don't count twice
tests.expr: expect(cohesionDensity({ edges: [{ from: 'A', to: 'B', callsPerDay: 1 }, { from: 'A', to: 'B', callsPerDay: 2 }] }, ['A', 'B'])).toBe(0.5)

items.explanation: Call-volume-weighted metrics like `internalCallRatio` can be dominated by one very chatty pair while the rest of the group barely talks to each other. `cohesionDensity` deliberately ignores volume and asks a structural question instead — of every possible directed relationship within the group, how many actually exist at all — which catches a group that's cohesive on paper but really just one busy pair plus several disconnected modules riding along.
items.reference:
cohesionDensity = distinct internal directed pairs / all possible directed pairs (n * (n-1)).

Why: a volume-weighted metric can hide a group that's really one busy pair plus disconnected riders.

items.prompt: Implement `cohesionDensity(graph, group)` again, and confirm it correctly handles a THREE-module group where only some of the six possible directed pairs are connected.

tests.description: 3-module group with 2 of 6 possible pairs connected gives 1/3
tests.expr: expect(cohesionDensity({ edges: [{ from: 'A', to: 'B', callsPerDay: 1 }, { from: 'B', to: 'C', callsPerDay: 1 }] }, ['A', 'B', 'C'])).toBe(1 / 3)

tests.description: edges touching a module outside the group are excluded from the count
tests.expr: expect(cohesionDensity({ edges: [{ from: 'A', to: 'B', callsPerDay: 1 }, { from: 'A', to: 'Z', callsPerDay: 1 }] }, ['A', 'B', 'C'])).toBe(1 / 6)

items.explanation: With 3 modules there are `3 * 2 = 6` possible directed pairs. Only edges where BOTH endpoints are members of `group` count toward the numerator — an edge reaching a module outside the group (like `A->Z` here) is excluded entirely, the same `inGroup.has(from) && inGroup.has(to)` check used throughout this unit's metrics.
items.reference:
cohesionDensity = distinct internal directed pairs / all possible directed pairs (n * (n-1)).

Why: a volume-weighted metric can hide a group that's really one busy pair plus disconnected riders.

items.prompt: Implement `cohesionDensity(graph, group)` a third time, verifying that a group with modules that never call each other at all (zero internal edges) correctly returns 0, not an error from dividing by zero.

tests.description: no internal edges at all returns exactly 0
tests.expr: expect(cohesionDensity({ edges: [{ from: 'A', to: 'Z', callsPerDay: 5 }] }, ['A', 'B'])).toBe(0)

tests.description: empty edges array with a valid group returns 0
tests.expr: expect(cohesionDensity({ edges: [] }, ['A', 'B', 'C'])).toBe(0)

items.explanation: When no edge has both endpoints inside `group`, `pairs` stays an empty Set, so the division is `0 / (n * (n - 1))` — a normal division by a positive denominator (guaranteed positive by the `n < 2` early return), never a divide-by-zero, and the result is exactly 0 as expected for a group with no internal relationships at all.

Why: a volume-weighted metric can hide a group that's really one busy pair plus disconnected riders.
